section.title: Seventy Years of Captivity
section.sectionRationale: This chapter is a hinge for the whole book: it looks back over twenty-three years of ignored warnings, fixes the coming exile at a specific length, seventy years, and then widens the lens from Judah alone to every nation, who must all drink the same cup of God's wrath from His hand.
section.thesis: Twenty-three years of patient warning have run out; Babylon's rule and Judah's exile are now fixed at seventy years, and that same cup of wrath, first pressed to Judah's lips, must be drunk by every nation on earth, for the LORD is bringing judgment on all mankind.
section.frameNote: Four movements: a summary of twenty-three years of unheeded prophetic warning, the seventy years of captivity decreed, the cup of wrath passed to every surrounding nation, and the LORD's roar of judgment against the whole earth.

verses.text: This is the word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah, which was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.
So the prophet Jeremiah spoke to all the people of Judah and all the residents of Jerusalem as follows:

“From the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon king of Judah until this very day, twenty-three years, the word of the LORD has come to me, and I have spoken to you again and again, but you have not listened.
And the LORD has sent all His servants the prophets to you again and again, but you have not listened or inclined your ear to hear.
The prophets told you, ‘Turn now, each of you, from your evil ways and deeds, and you can dwell in the land that the LORD has given to you and your fathers forever and ever.
Do not follow other gods to serve and worship them, and do not provoke Me to anger with the works of your hands. Then I will do you no harm.’
‘But to your own harm, you have not listened to Me,’ declares the LORD, ‘so you have provoked Me to anger with the works of your hands.’

units.label: Seventy years decreed
units.note: a fixed length to the discipline

verses.text: Therefore this is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘Because you have not obeyed My words,

behold, I will summon all the families of the north, declares the LORD, and I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, whom I will bring against this land, against its residents, and against all the surrounding nations. So I will devote them to destruction and make them an object of horror and contempt, an everlasting desolation.
Moreover, I will banish from them the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the lamp.
And this whole land will become a desolate wasteland, and these nations will serve the king of Babylon for {{shivim|seventy years}}.
But when seventy years are complete, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their guilt, declares the LORD, and I will make it an everlasting desolation.
I will bring upon that land all the words I have pronounced against it, all that is written in this book, which Jeremiah has prophesied against all the nations.
For many nations and great kings will enslave them, and I will repay them according to their deeds and according to the work of their hands.’”

units.label: The cup of wrath for all nations

verses.text: This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, said to me: “Take from My hand this {{kos|cup}} of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink from it.
And they will drink and stagger and go out of their minds, because of the sword that I will send among them.”
So I took the cup from the LORD's hand and made all the nations drink from it, each one to whom the LORD had sent me,
to make them a ruin, an object of horror and contempt and cursing, as they are to this day, Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, its kings and officials;
Pharaoh king of Egypt, his officials, his leaders, and all his people;
all the mixed tribes; all the kings of Uz; all the kings of the Philistines: Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod;
Edom, Moab, and the Ammonites;
all the kings of Tyre and Sidon; the kings of the coastlands across the sea;
Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who cut the corners of their hair;
all the kings of Arabia, and all the kings of the mixed tribes who dwell in the desert;
all the kings of Zimri, Elam, and Media;
all the kings of the north, both near and far, one after another, all the kingdoms on the face of the earth. And after all of them, the king of Sheshach will drink it too.
“Then you are to tell them that this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘Drink, get drunk, and vomit. Fall down and never get up again, because of the sword I will send among you.’
If they refuse to take the cup from your hand and drink it, you are to tell them that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘You most certainly must drink it!

For behold, I am beginning to bring disaster on the city that bears My Name, so how could you possibly go unpunished? You will not go unpunished, for I am calling down a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth, declares the LORD of Hosts.’

units.label: The LORD's roar against all the earth

verses.text:
So you are to prophesy all these words against them and say to them: 
‘The LORD will roar from on high; He will raise His voice from His holy habitation. He will roar loudly over His pasture; like those who tread the grapes, He will call out with a shout against all the inhabitants of the earth.
The tumult will resound to the ends of the earth because the LORD brings a charge against the nations. He brings judgment on all mankind and puts the wicked to the sword,’” declares the LORD.

This is what the LORD of Hosts says: 
“Behold! Disaster is spreading from nation to nation; a mighty storm is rising from the ends of the earth.”
Those slain by the LORD on that day will be spread from one end of the earth to the other. They will not be mourned, gathered, or buried. They will be like dung lying on the ground.
Wail, you shepherds, and cry out; roll in the dust, you leaders of the flock. For the days of your slaughter have come; you will fall and be shattered like fine pottery.
Flight will evade the shepherds, and escape will elude the leaders of the flock.

Hear the cry of the shepherds, the wailing of the leaders of the flock, 
for the LORD is destroying their pasture.
The peaceful meadows have been silenced because of the LORD's burning anger.
He has left His den like a lion, for their land has been made a desolation by the sword of the oppressor, and because of the fierce anger of the LORD.

shivim.gloss: Seventy years, the fixed length God sets on Judah's exile under Babylon. Far from an open-ended punishment, it is a bounded discipline with a promised end, later confirmed as fulfilled in Daniel 9:2 and cited by Zechariah 1:12, showing God's judgments come with a measured limit, not limitless wrath.

kos.gloss: Cup, here the cup of the wine of God's wrath that every nation, starting with Jerusalem itself, must drink in turn. This image of a cup of judgment recurs throughout Scripture and finds its most solemn use in Christ's own agonized prayer in Gethsemane over the cup He was about to drink on the world's behalf.

basic.context: Jeremiah looks back over twenty-three years of faithfully warning Judah, only to be ignored again and again, and now announces that the coming Babylonian exile has a fixed length, seventy years. But the chapter does not stop with Judah; God hands Jeremiah a cup of wrath that every surrounding nation, and finally the whole earth, must drink, showing that Judah's judgment is part of a far larger reckoning God is bringing on all mankind.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage combines specific, datable prophecy, the seventy years, later confirmed exactly in Daniel 9:2, with a much broader universal scope, judgment on all mankind, verse 31. Readers should hold both together: God's word here is precise enough to be historically verified, yet its ultimate horizon is not Judah alone but every nation and every wicked deed on earth.
basic.originalLanguages: The exile is fixed at shivim shanah, seventy years, a real, countable discipline with a real end, not endless punishment. And the image running through the chapter's center is the kos, the cup, of God's wrath, first pressed to Judah's own lips before every nation on earth is required to drink from the same hand, an image later taken up in its most solemn form by Christ Himself in Gethsemane.
basic.typology: The cup of wrath that every nation must drink anticipates the ultimate cup of divine judgment, which Christ prays might pass from Him in Gethsemane, yet willingly drinks on behalf of all who trust in Him. The fixed seventy years, ending in restoration, anticipates the pattern of all divine discipline in Scripture, bounded, purposeful, and always aimed at eventual mercy for those who turn back.
basic.christ: Christ's agonized prayer in Gethsemane, 'let this cup pass from Me,' Matthew 26:39, draws directly on this very image of the cup of God's wrath that Jeremiah describes every nation as needing to drink; Christ instead drinks it fully on behalf of His people, so that those united to Him need not drink it themselves. The LORD's roar of judgment against all mankind here finds its answer in the gospel, where that judgment falls instead on Christ for all who receive Him.
basic.god: God is patient beyond what seems reasonable, sending prophet after prophet for twenty-three years before finally acting, yet He is also universally just, holding not only Judah but every nation, Egypt, Philistia, Edom, Moab, Babylon itself, accountable to the same standard of righteousness. His judgments, though severe, are also measured, fixed at seventy years rather than left open-ended, revealing mercy even within wrath.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 9:2 confirms Jeremiah's seventy years as a specific, fulfilled prophecy that Daniel himself studied and prayed over. Matthew 26:39 shows Christ praying over the same image of a cup of divine wrath, which He then drinks on behalf of sinners. Isaiah 51:17-22 uses the same cup imagery, later promising it will be taken from Jerusalem's hand and given instead to her tormentors. Revelation 14:10 describes final judgment using the identical image of the cup of God's wrath.
basic.oneStory: The cup of wrath that every nation must drink shows that Judah's judgment was never a private matter between God and one people; it previews a reckoning that touches all mankind. That universal judgment finds its resolution at the cross, where Christ drinks the cup of wrath in full so that everyone who trusts in Him is spared from having to drink it themselves.

context.literary:
Jeremiah 25 is the hinge of the whole book. It closes the first great part, the long cycle of warnings to Judah that began at the call, and it opens the way to the narratives of chapters 26 to 45 and the oracles against the nations at the end. It is also dated more precisely than almost any other chapter: the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the first of Nebuchadnezzar, 25:1, which is the year Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish, 46:2. The prophet looks back over twenty-three years, forward over seventy, and outward over the whole earth.

The chapter has four movements. In 25:1-7 the prophet reviews a quarter century of unheeded warning. In 25:8-14 the sentence is passed: the north will come, the land will be silent, and the nations will serve Babylon for seventy years. In 25:15-29 a symbolic act, the cup, gives the judgment a universal scope. In 25:30-38 a poem of the LORD's roar closes the whole.

Notice the movement from the particular to the universal. The chapter begins with 'all the people of Judah' and ends with 'all the inhabitants of the earth', and the list of nations in verses 18 to 26 is an extended roll call that moves in widening circles from Jerusalem to Egypt, to the near neighbours, to Arabia, to the peoples of the far north, and finally to Babylon itself. The cup passes from hand to hand until it reaches the one who has been holding it.

The poem at the end uses the same figure of a lion, a storm and a harvest of grapes to describe a God whose roar can be heard from the ends of the earth. The shepherds who wail in verses 34 to 36 are the leaders of the nations, and the language echoes Jeremiah 23, where the shepherds of Judah were judged. The chapter also resumes the sound of the earlier dirges: the voices of the bride and bridegroom are silenced, 25:10, as they were in 7:34 and 16:9, a refrain that will return in the book of consolation as the sound of joy restored, 33:10-11.
context.historical:
The date is the year 605 BC. In that year Nebuchadnezzar defeated Pharaoh Necho at Carchemish and became king of Babylon on his father's death, and a new world power took the place of Assyria and Egypt. For Jeremiah's hearers the news was still new, and many in Judah assumed that Egypt would recover. The prophet tells them that the rise of Babylon is God's doing, and that He calls Nebuchadnezzar 'My servant', 25:9, an astonishing title for a pagan conqueror, repeated in 27:6 and 43:10.

The twenty-three years begin in the thirteenth year of Josiah, which is the year of Jeremiah's call, 1:2, so the prophet has been speaking since about 627 BC. That span takes in Josiah's reform, the collapse of Assyria, Josiah's death at Megiddo and the three-month reign of Shallum, and the first years of Jehoiakim. The phrase translated 'again and again' is an idiom that means literally rising early and speaking, as the BSB footnote says, and it pictures a God who gets up at dawn to send His messengers. The prophets before Jeremiah, the 'servants', had said the same.

The nations listed are the real peoples of the Near East of Jeremiah's day. Uz, Edom, Moab and Ammon lay east and south of Judah, the Philistine cities of Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and Ashdod lay on the coast, and Tyre and Sidon were the great Phoenician ports. Dedan, Tema and Buz were Arabian oasis peoples, and Elam and Media lay far to the east. 'All who cut the corners of their hair' describes desert tribes who shaved the temples, a custom Jeremiah mentions again in 9:26. Most of these appear again in the oracles of chapters 46 to 49.

The final name, 'the king of Sheshach', is a cipher. Sheshach is a way of writing Babel using a reversed alphabet, and Jeremiah 51:41 sets the two names in parallel, so everyone who knew the code knew who it meant. The prophet thus names Babylon last in the list and in code, as the one who must drink after all the others.
context.canonical:
The seventy years were first set in Jeremiah's own ministry in the letter of chapter 29, which promises that when 'Babylon's seventy years are complete' God will attend to the exiles and restore them, 29:10. The Chronicler later reads the whole exile through the number: the land 'enjoyed its Sabbath rest all the days of the desolation, until seventy years were completed', 2 Chronicles 36:21, which echoes Leviticus 26:34-35, where the land was promised its Sabbaths if Israel was driven out. The number thus holds both the prophetic word and the Torah's warning together.

Daniel takes up the prophecy in Daniel 9:2, understanding 'from the sacred books' that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years, and he responds in confession and prayer. Ezra 1:1 begins with the stirring of Cyrus 'to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah', and Zechariah speaks of seventy years in two places, 1:12 and 7:5. The seventy years is one of the most quoted numbers in the Old Testament.

The cup of wrath belongs to a tradition of prophetic language. Psalm 75:8 speaks of a cup in the LORD's hand that all the wicked of the earth drink down to the dregs. Isaiah 51:17-22 says Jerusalem has drunk the cup and promises that it will be taken from her hand, Habakkuk 2:16 says that the cup in the LORD's right hand comes round to Babylon, and Lamentations 4:21 says that it will pass to Edom as well. Jeremiah 49:12 and 51:7 are part of the book's own development of the figure.

The New Testament draws on all of this. Jesus asks James and John whether they can drink the cup that He is to drink, Matthew 20:22, and prays in Gethsemane that it pass from Him, Matthew 26:39. In Revelation the figure returns for the last time: the nations drink the wine of God's anger, Revelation 14:10, and Babylon is given the cup of the fury of His wrath, Revelation 16:19. The silencing of the bride and bridegroom, the millstone and the lamp, which is Jeremiah 25:10, is quoted almost word for word in Revelation 18:22-23.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jeremiah's aim was to make the judgment on Judah understandable and bearable. He first appeals to the record, twenty-three years of warning, in order to show that God had not acted hastily and that the people had no excuse. The point of verses 3 to 7 is that the exile is the answer to a refusal and not a surprise.

Then he gives the judgment a shape. Seventy years has a start and an end, and the people who would be in Babylon needed to know that the story did not end there. The announcement was meant to prevent two mistakes: the false hope of the prophets who said the trouble would pass quickly, and the despair of those who thought it would never end. In chapter 29 he applies it explicitly, and tells the exiles to settle in for a long time and trust that God will visit them.

By extending the cup to every nation he also meant the people of Judah to see that they were not singled out for cruelty. The same God who judged them would judge the Egyptians, the Philistines and Babylon itself. For a people tempted to think of Babylon's power as ultimate, this was a word of reassurance: the empire that now seemed unstoppable was itself drinking from a cup.

And he meant the passage to unsettle any who supposed that being God's own city offered protection. The key sentence is 25:29: 'I am beginning to bring disaster on the city that bears My Name, so how could you possibly go unpunished?' If God begins with His own, no one else can assume they are exempt.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records a prophetic sermon and a symbolic act. The prophet is told to take the cup and make the nations drink, 25:15, and the narration says that he did, 25:17, though it is not likely that he carried a literal cup from capital to capital. The scene is a vision, or an acted parable, announcing what God will do. The reader should not look for an instruction to repeat the act.

The seventy years are a specific forecast about a specific period, and they were fulfilled in history. The passage does not give a formula for dating other events. The cup language describes God's judgment, and the detail of verses 33 to 38, with its picture of unburied slain and ruined shepherds, is poetic and describes the character of the judgment, not a schedule.

What carries over is the pattern of divine patience followed by judgment, the truth that no nation is exempt from accountability to God, and the assurance that judgment has limits. The passage also teaches us to look at nations and empires with a sober eye. Power is on loan, and the power that humbles others will be humbled. At the same time, Christians should be cautious about reading a specific present-day nation into the list of verses 18 to 26. The chapter names ancient peoples, and where it speaks of 'all the kingdoms on the face of the earth' it is making a universal claim without drawing a map.

debates.question: How should the seventy years be counted, and does it matter for the chapter's message?

views.label: From the first deportation, 605 BC, to the decree of Cyrus, 538 BC
views.case: This reading counts roughly seventy years of Babylonian dominance beginning with Daniel's own deportation, matching Daniel 9:2's application of the prophecy to his own generation nearing its end.

views.label: From the temple's destruction, 586 BC, to its rebuilding completion, 516 BC
views.case: This reading counts seventy years of the temple lying in ruins specifically, matching the concern of Zechariah 1:12 with mourning over Jerusalem and the temple during that same span.

debates.bearing: Either calculation lands within a real, verifiable historical window, and the chapter's main point, that God's judgment is bounded and will end in restoration, holds regardless of which starting point is preferred.

debates.question: Is the number seventy exact, or a round figure for a full span?

views.label: An approximately literal count
views.case: The prophecy is repeated in 29:10 and read by Daniel as a countable period, and the Chronicler ties it to the land's Sabbaths, 2 Chronicles 36:21. Between Nebuchadnezzar's rise and the fall of Babylon in 539 BC is about two thirds of a century, and between the temple's fall and its rebuilding is about seventy years, so the number matches events without strain.

views.label: A conventional figure for a lifetime
views.case: Isaiah 23:15 speaks of seventy years for Tyre as 'the span of a king's life', and Psalm 90:10 treats seventy years as the span of a human life. On this view the number stands for one full generation of discipline, long enough for those who rebelled to pass away, whether or not it is arithmetically exact.

debates.bearing: The two views are not far apart. The number is real enough that Daniel, Ezra and Zechariah treated it as a fulfilled promise, and generous enough in its meaning that it speaks of a measured, purposeful period. Both agree that the exile had a set end because God had set it.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 9 says that God will 'devote' the land and its people 'to destruction'. The BSB footnote explains the Hebrew behind this: forms of cherem refer to the giving over of things or persons, either by destroying them or by giving them as an offering. The word belongs to holy war. In Joshua it is what Israel does to Jericho, setting a city apart for God, and here it is turned against Israel. The people who were to carry out the ban on the Canaanites are themselves put under it. The vocabulary of conquest is taken from the book of Joshua and turned back on those who had forgotten its terms.

God calls Nebuchadnezzar 'My servant', 25:9. The Hebrew 'eved is the word used of Moses, of David and of the prophets, and applied elsewhere in the Old Testament to Israel itself. It does not say that Nebuchadnezzar is righteous. It says that he is God's agent, doing a task God has assigned, and that his power exists because the LORD gave it, as 27:6 says. The same king who will later be called a destroyer is here a tool in the hand of the One who sends.

The pairing in verse 10, the voice of joy and gladness, the voice of the bride and bridegroom, the millstones and the lamp, is a list of the daily sounds of a settled village. By naming ordinary signs of life rather than great ones, Jeremiah makes the judgment domestic: the land will fall silent in the way a home does when no one is there. The same list is used in Revelation 18:22-23 as the sign of Babylon's final silence.

Verse 15 calls the cup a cup 'of the wine of wrath', and verse 16 says the nations will 'stagger and go out of their minds'. The language is that of intoxication. The nations lose their footing and their senses, and the image makes judgment something from which one cannot stand upright. The cup is not poured out but handed round, and its being 'taken from My hand' stresses that it is the LORD who administers it.

Finally the cipher of verse 26. Sheshach is Babel written in a reversed alphabet, the substitution known as atbash, in which the first letter of the alphabet stands for the last and the second for the second last. Its use here, and again in 51:41, shows the prophet using a device that those in the know could read.

typology.type: The cup of wrath handed to the nations
typology.fulfillment: The cup that Jeremiah carries from nation to nation is the first full development of a figure that runs through the prophets. It pictures judgment as something that must be drunk to the dregs. In Christ the figure becomes personal. Jesus asks whether His disciples can drink the cup that He is to drink, Matthew 20:22, and prays that it pass from Him, Matthew 26:39, and then says, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?', John 18:11. The escalation is that what the nations were made to drink, the Son drinks on their behalf, so that Isaiah's promise that the cup is taken from Jerusalem's hand, Isaiah 51:22, is fulfilled in Him. The type falls short in that Jeremiah's cup is administered by the prophet, while Christ both gives and drinks.

The exile is a measured period of discipline with a fixed end. It is a type of God's way with His people in every age: a limited, purposeful discipline that ends in restoration. Daniel's prayer shows how it works, as he confesses sin and asks for mercy, Daniel 9:3-19, and receives a further word about the history that is still to come, Daniel 9:24. In Christ the pattern is that the long night of exile ends in the coming of the Son, Galatians 4:4. The exile's end was the decree of Cyrus, a partial return; the true end is the return from sin and death that Christ accomplishes.

typology.type: The land lying desolate to enjoy its sabbaths
typology.fulfillment: Behind the seventy years stands the law of the land's rest, Leviticus 26:34-35. The land is given the Sabbaths that Israel had not kept, so that the exile is a kind of enforced Sabbath. The Sabbath pattern finds its fulfilment in Christ, who says 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest', Matthew 11:28, and in the rest that remains for the people of God, Hebrews 4:9-10. The correspondence is that rest is God's gift and will be had. The pattern falls short because the land's rest was imposed by exile, while Christ's rest is offered freely.

typology.type: Judgment beginning at the house of God
typology.fulfillment: The LORD says that He is beginning to bring disaster on the city that bears His Name, 25:29. The principle is that those nearest to God's presence are judged first. Peter applies it to the church: it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God, 1 Peter 4:17. In Christ the principle is fulfilled at the cross, where judgment falls on the One who is most closely identified with God's name, so that those who trust Him are spared. The type falls short in that Jerusalem bore its own judgment, whereas Christ bears the judgment that others deserved.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ most directly through the cup. When Jesus kneels in Gethsemane and asks that the cup pass from Him, He is taking up a figure that the prophets had made familiar, the cup of the wine of wrath that God hands to the nations. Jeremiah's cup is the fullest early form of it: the cup that every nation must drink, and that no one can refuse, 25:28. The disciples who say they can drink the cup do not understand what they are saying, Matthew 20:22. What Jesus faces is not mere suffering but this cup, the judgment of God on the sin of the world.

That is what makes the cross the answer to Jeremiah 25. The universal judgment of verses 29 to 33, in which no nation is exempt, is not set aside but borne. Paul says that God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice, 'in order to demonstrate His righteousness', Romans 3:25. Christ became a curse for us, Galatians 3:13, and by God's grace tasted death for everyone, Hebrews 2:9. Those who trust Him are not made to drink what He has drunk, which is the promise Isaiah had given Jerusalem: 'From that goblet, the cup of My fury, you will never drink again', Isaiah 51:22.

The chapter also shows Christ as the One in whom God's patience reaches its limit and its answer together. For twenty-three years the LORD rose early and sent His servants, and they were not heeded. The parable of the tenants says the same of the whole history, that the owner sent servant after servant and finally his son, Matthew 21:33-39. Christ is the last in the line of those whom God sent. The word of the prophets was refused, and the Son is sent.

The universal scope of the chapter looks toward the universal scope of the gospel. If the cup is for all nations, so is the offer of the gospel, and Jesus sends His disciples to all nations, Matthew 28:19. The nations that were summoned to judgment are summoned to repentance. The final scenes of Revelation show that both are true: the cup of wrath is poured on those who refuse, Revelation 14:10, and the nations bring their glory into the city of the Lamb, Revelation 21:24.

Finally, the seventy years show a Lord who keeps appointed times. The promise of an end to the exile is kept, and the greater promise is kept with it. Paul says that when the time had fully come, God sent His Son, Galatians 4:4. The long silence that began with the exile and reached its end under Cyrus is only the first of the endings.

A caution: Jeremiah 25 is not a coded prophecy of the crucifixion. The cup is a prophetic image in its own right, and the New Testament takes it up because Jesus Himself did. The link is the one He made in Gethsemane.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God of astonishing patience. 'The LORD has sent all His servants the prophets to you again and again', 25:4. For twenty-three years Jeremiah spoke, and for generations before that others spoke, and the pattern of getting up early to send a message is the pattern of a God who does not want to punish. The judgment is delayed not because He is slow but because He is giving time to repent. This is the God of Exodus 34:6, slow to anger, who nonetheless does not leave the guilty unpunished.

He is sovereign over empires. The same God who gives Nebuchadnezzar his victories is the one who sets the length of his rule, 25:11-12. Babylon is raised up, used and put down by a decision that was made before it began. Kingdoms are drawn in the book of Jeremiah as characters in a drama whose author is God, and this is the central teaching of the political theology of the Old Testament.

He is just to every nation. The cup passes to Egypt and to Philistia, to Edom and Moab and Ammon, to the coastlands and the desert tribes, and to Babylon itself. No one is left out, and no one has a patron deity who can spare him. The same standard of justice applies to the people who have the law and to those who do not, though those who have the law are judged first, 25:29. This is a God who is not the tribal deity of Judah but the Lord of the earth.

He is moderate in His judgments as well as fierce. The seventy years is a limit, and the sentence on Babylon, 25:12, shows that even the instrument of discipline will be accountable for its pride. The one who is used is not thereby excused. Judgment on the oppressor is the other side of mercy to the oppressed, and the Chronicler and Daniel both read the end of the seventy years as God's faithfulness.

He is fearsome. The poem of verses 30 to 38 is among the most terrible in the book. The LORD roars like a lion and treads the grapes, and the slain are spread from one end of the earth to the other. The picture is not meant to be softened. It insists that God's anger is real, and that it is directed against evil, 25:31. A faith that cannot speak of this has lost part of the Bible's testimony about who God is.

And He keeps His word to the last detail. The chapter's prediction is specific, and Daniel and Ezra read its fulfilment from the sacred books. A God who names a number and keeps it is a God who can be trusted with the larger promises.

For worship, the chapter calls us to fear the LORD rightly and to be thankful that the cup has been drunk for us. It teaches us to pray with Daniel, who read the book, saw the number and turned to confession.

crossReferences.note: The letter to the exiles takes up the seventy years and gives them their promise: when Babylon's seventy years are complete, God will attend to them and bring them home. Chapter 25 announces the sentence, and chapter 29 shows what it means for the people who have to live inside it.

The Chronicler reads the exile through the seventy years and through the land's Sabbaths. The land lay desolate until seventy years were completed, in fulfilment of the word through Jeremiah. It is the historian's confirmation that the number was kept.

The Torah warns that if Israel is driven out, the land will enjoy its Sabbaths all the days it lies desolate. Jeremiah's seventy years are the working out of this warning, and show that the exile is covenant discipline and not an accident of politics.

Daniel, living in Babylon, reads Jeremiah and understands that the desolation of Jerusalem will last seventy years. His response is not calculation but prayer. It shows how the first readers were meant to use the prophecy, as a summons to confess and to seek the LORD.

Jerusalem has drunk the cup of the LORD's fury to the dregs, and the LORD now says He has removed it from her hand and will put it in the hand of her tormentors. It is the other side of Jeremiah 25: the cup that passes to the nations is also taken from God's own people.

Babylon is a gold cup in the LORD's hand, making the whole earth drunk. The instrument of the cup in chapter 25 becomes the one who must finally drink, which is how the book resolves the cipher of 'the king of Sheshach' in verse 26.

In Gethsemane Jesus prays that the cup pass from Him, yet not as He wills but as the Father wills. The cup He means is the one of the prophets, the wrath of God against sin, and it explains why He is in such distress.

When Peter draws his sword at the arrest, Jesus tells him to put it away and asks, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' The cup is given by the Father, as in Jeremiah 25:15 it is taken from the LORD's hand, and Christ accepts it.

Those who worship the beast will drink the wine of God's anger, poured undiluted into the cup of His wrath. The final judgment is described in the vocabulary of Jeremiah 25, and shows that the cup is not finished with in the Old Testament.

The silencing of the musicians, the millstone, the lamp and the voices of bride and bridegroom is applied to the final Babylon. John takes the list of Jeremiah 25:10 and uses it for the last fall of the city that opposes God.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's account of the world begins with nations that God made from one man, Acts 17:26, and moves quickly to nations that gather themselves against Him at Babel, Genesis 11. Babylon, the city of Babel, is the name for the human project of building a name apart from God. Jeremiah 25 is the moment where that project is allowed to win a battle and is then told that it has a limit. It is a scene from the middle of the story, where history is run by the God who made it.

The chapter answers questions from earlier in the story. Why was Israel, rescued from Egypt and settled in a land, driven out? Because the covenant had warnings built into it, Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28, and because twenty-three years of messengers had gone unheeded. And why does a pagan empire rule the people of God? Because God sent it, and because He has appointed its time.

It also sets up much of what follows. The seventy years are the horizon of the exile, which is the horizon of Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai and Zechariah. The cup of wrath is the figure that will be taken into the gospels and into Revelation. And the universal sweep of the judgment is the background of the nations' hope, since a God who judges all nations is the God who can bless them, Genesis 12:3.

The story reaches its centre at the cross, where the cup of wrath is drunk by the Son, and the decree that releases captives is fulfilled in a greater return. Christ is the answer to the exile in a deeper sense than Cyrus was, because He brings people out of the captivity of sin.

And it ends in a world where no cup is left to drink. Babylon falls for the last time, Revelation 18, and the bride's voice sounds in the city whose gates are never shut, Revelation 19:7 and 21:25. The sound of the millstone and of the lamp, silenced in Jeremiah 25:10, is restored where God Himself is the light, Revelation 22:5. The people who were told that judgment begins at the house of God are the people who see, at the end, that there is no curse any more, Revelation 22:3.

quiz.q: How long had Jeremiah been prophesying to Judah before this chapter, according to verse 3?

options.text: Twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of Josiah until this very day.
options.note: This detail underscores the sheer patience of God's warnings before judgment finally falls.

options.text: Only a few months.
options.note: The text specifies a much longer period of twenty-three years.

options.text: Seventy years, the same as the length of exile.
options.note: Seventy years is the length of the coming exile, not the length of Jeremiah's ministry up to this point.

options.text: Since before Jeremiah was born.
options.note: The twenty-three years is measured from Jeremiah's own call, not before his birth.

quiz.q: What is significant about the seventy years fixed for Judah's captivity?

options.text: It is a bounded, purposeful discipline with a definite end, later confirmed as historically fulfilled in Daniel 9:2.
options.note: The judgment is real and severe, yet limited rather than open-ended, showing mercy within justice.

options.text: It means the exile would never actually end.
options.note: The passage specifies a fixed term, after which Babylon itself would be judged and the exile would end.

options.text: It refers to seventy individual people taken into exile.
options.note: Seventy years is a length of time, not a count of individuals.

options.text: It was never actually fulfilled in later biblical history.
options.note: Daniel 9:2 shows this prophecy being read and applied as a real, fulfilled timeframe.

quiz.q: Who is commanded to drink the cup of the LORD's wrath in this chapter?

options.text: Jerusalem first, and then every surrounding nation and kingdom on the face of the earth.
options.note: Verses 18 to 26 list an extensive roster of nations, beginning with Jerusalem itself, all required to drink.

options.text: Only Babylon, with no other nation included.
options.note: The list explicitly includes many nations beyond Babylon, including Jerusalem itself first.

options.text: Only the nations who had never heard of the God of Israel.
options.note: The list includes Jerusalem and Judah, who certainly knew the LORD, showing knowledge of God does not exempt anyone from this judgment.

options.text: No one; the cup is only a metaphor with no actual recipients named.
options.note: The chapter names an extensive, specific list of nations required to drink the cup.

quiz.q: What is the scope of the judgment described in verses 30 to 31?

options.text: The LORD brings a charge against the nations and judgment on all mankind, not Judah alone.
options.note: Verse 31 explicitly states 'He brings judgment on all mankind,' a universal scope beyond any single nation.

options.text: It is limited strictly to the city of Jerusalem.
options.note: The passage explicitly widens the scope to 'all the inhabitants of the earth' and 'all mankind.'

options.text: It applies only to religious leaders, not ordinary people.
options.note: The judgment described is universal in scope, not limited to any one class of people.

options.text: It describes only a future judgment with no present application.
options.note: The judgment described is announced as imminent and historical, following directly from the twenty-three years of warning already given.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament pick up the image of the cup of wrath from this chapter?

options.text: Christ prays over this same cup of divine wrath in Gethsemane and then drinks it fully at the cross on behalf of His people.
options.note: Matthew 26:39 draws directly on this image, showing Christ bearing the judgment described here so believers do not have to.

options.text: The New Testament never references the image of a cup of wrath.
options.note: Matthew 26:39 and Revelation 14:10 both use this exact image directly.

options.text: It is used only to describe a literal cup used at the Last Supper with no connection to judgment.
options.note: While the Last Supper cup is a separate image, Christ's Gethsemane prayer specifically concerns the cup of wrath, not a literal drinking vessel from the meal.

options.text: It is applied only to unbelievers with no connection to Christ Himself.
options.note: The Gospels show Christ Himself drinking this cup of wrath on behalf of His people, not only describing it as applying to others.

questions: God sent prophet after prophet for twenty-three years before judgment fell. Is there a warning you have been hearing repeatedly that you have not yet heeded?
The seventy years of exile were painful but bounded, aimed at eventual restoration. How does knowing God's discipline has a purpose and an end change how you endure a hard season?
Every nation, not Judah alone, had to drink the cup of wrath; no one could claim exemption. Where might you be assuming you are exempt from accountability that actually applies to you too?
Christ drank the cup of wrath fully so His people would not have to. How does knowing that change the weight you carry over your own sin and guilt?
The LORD's judgment reaches 'all mankind', not one nation only. How does that shape the way you think about God's justice toward the whole world, not just your own circle?

translationNotes.note: 'Seventy years' is best understood as a round, symbolically complete number describing a full generation of Babylonian dominance, while also matching closely with the actual historical span later confirmed by Daniel.

'The cup of the wine of wrath' is a common prophetic image for inescapable divine judgment, appearing also in Isaiah, Habakkuk, and Revelation, always describing a reckoning no one can refuse to drink.

'Sheshach' is widely understood as a coded name for Babylon, using a Hebrew cipher called atbash; naming Babylon last and by a veiled name underscores that even Babylon itself, the instrument of judgment, would not escape drinking the same cup.
